overview.text:
Amritsar takes its name from the Amrit Sarovar, the 'Pool of Nectar' around the Golden Temple — the holiest site of Sikhism. The city grew from a settlement founded in the 1570s by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru, and its free community kitchen, the langar, feeds visitors of every faith day and night.

A short walk from the temple lie Jallianwala Bagh, where British troops fired on a crowd on 13 April 1919, and the Partition Museum in the old Town Hall, the world's first museum devoted to the 1947 Partition. Heritage Street links the Town Hall to the Golden Temple. In the evening, the Beating Retreat ceremony at the Attari–Wagah border, about 28–30 km away, draws big, cheering crowds. Amritsar is also one of India's great food cities, famous for its kulcha.

best_time.text: October to March is the most pleasant time to visit, although the city welcomes visitors year-round. Summers, from April to June, can reach 45 °C, and the monsoon runs from July to September.

how_to_reach.text: Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport serves Amritsar with domestic and international flights; it accounted for 1.79% of foreign tourist arrivals by air in 2024. The Attari–Wagah border is about 28–30 km west of the city on the Grand Trunk Road.

overview.text:
The Golden Temple, or Sri Harmandir Sahib, is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism. Guru Arjan Dev built it to house the Sikh scripture, and Maharaja Ranjit Singh rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809, covering the sanctum in gold in 1830. Its four entrances symbolise openness to people of every caste, creed and religion.

Pilgrims walk the marble path around the sacred pool, the Amrit Sarovar. Facing the sanctum is the Akal Takht, the foremost seat of Sikh temporal and spiritual authority. The langar, run by volunteers, serves about 100,000 free vegetarian meals a day. An underground Interpretation Centre introduces Sikhism through short films, with free English headsets. The temple is at its most vibrant at Vaisakhi, Guru Nanak's birthday and Diwali, when it is lit with lamps.

overview.text:
On 13 April 1919, troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired on a crowd gathered in this walled garden, including people peacefully protesting the Rowlatt Act. The exact death toll is still debated: hundreds were killed and over a thousand injured. The massacre became a turning point in India's struggle for independence.

Today the garden is a national memorial, a short walk from the Golden Temple. You enter through the same narrow passage, and can still see bullet-marked walls and the well where people jumped to escape. The red-stone Flame of Liberty rises 30 feet, and a small museum, the Martyrs' Gallery, tells the story of the freedom struggle.

overview.text: Opened in 2017 in Amritsar's historic Town Hall, the Partition Museum is the world's first museum devoted to the Partition of 1947. Its 14 galleries trace the years leading up to Partition and its aftermath through photographs, letters, everyday objects carried by refugees and over 100 recorded oral-history interviews. It is a 5–7 minute walk from the Golden Temple, at the start of Heritage Street.

images.alt: Packed spectator stands under a huge Indian flag at the Attari–Wagah border
images.caption: Attari–Wagah border

overview.text: Every evening just before sunset, India's Border Security Force and the Pakistan Rangers perform the Beating Retreat ceremony at the Attari–Wagah border, a tradition held here since 1959. Soldiers march with high kicks and stamps, crowds on both sides cheer, and the two flags are lowered in unison before the gates close. The border is about 28–30 km from Amritsar on the Grand Trunk Road; Punjab Tourism recommends reaching the gallery at least 45 minutes early for a good view.

items.body: The joint check post stands on the historic Grand Trunk Road, where India's National Highway 1 begins; the ceremony began here in 1959.
The evening ends with the flags folded, a brief handshake between the soldiers and the closing of the gates.
On occasions such as Eid, Diwali and Independence Days, the two sides traditionally exchange sweets and greetings.

items.title: Travel advisories
items.body: As of October 2026, the UK government advises against all travel within 10 km of the India–Pakistan border — this includes the ceremony site. The border crossing is closed except for the daily ceremony. Check your own government's advice and your insurance before you go.

items.title: Timings
items.body: Punjab Tourism lists 4:30–5:30 pm (October–March) and 6:30–7:30 pm (April–September). Timings follow sunset — confirm locally.

overview.text: Gobindgarh Fort was built in the 1760s by Gujjar Singh Bhangi and rebuilt by Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Long held by the army, it opened to the public in 2017 and now hosts exhibitions and shows, including Sher-e-Punjab, a 15-minute 7D film on Ranjit Singh. Punjab Tourism lists it as open 10 am–10 pm, with tickets from Rs 180–649 for Indians and Rs 250–1,000 for foreigners; go in the evening to see the shows.
